Learning Objectives

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • 01Define spatial interpolation and explain how it estimates unknown values from known sample points.
  • 02Describe common sampling approaches and explain why sampling pattern and density matter for interpolation.
  • 03Explain the main assumptions of interpolation, including continuity and spatial autocorrelation.
  • 04Compare basic interpolation methods, including Voronoi/Thiessen polygons, fixed radius, and inverse distance weighting (IDW).
  • 05Evaluate interpolation results by recognizing sources of error and the role of RMSE in assessing accuracy.

What is spatial interpolation?

We can measure a phenomenon only at the places we actually sample — but we often need a value everywhere. Interpolation is how we get from a handful of points to a full surface.

Spatial interpolation is a technique used to estimate unknown values at specific geographic locations based on known values at sample locations.

Samples typically come from field measurements or observational data collected at specific locations. Example applications include environmental monitoring stations, soil or water quality testing sites, and survey and field data collection.

Sampling approaches

Below, you will find some example sampling approaches:

  • ·Random sampling: Sample locations are placed completely at random across the study area, so points may cluster in some places and leave gaps in others.
  • ·Systematic random sampling: The area is divided into a regular grid, and one sample is placed at a random location within each grid cell, giving more even coverage while still keeping some randomness.
  • ·Systematic centric sampling: Samples are taken at the center of every grid cell, producing very regular, evenly spaced coverage with no randomness.
  • ·Systematic unaligned sampling: The area is divided into grid cells, but sample positions vary independently by row or column, so coverage stays fairly even while avoiding the rigid pattern of perfectly centered points.

Spatial interpolation assumptions

Interpolation only makes sense if two things are true about the phenomenon we are mapping:

  • 01The phenomenon is continuous: the variable of interest changes gradually over space.
  • 02The phenomenon is spatially autocorrelated: locations that are close have similar values.
Tobler’s First Law of Geography
“Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.” This is the same spatial autocorrelation you measured with Moran’s I back in Week 8 — here it stops being something we detect and becomes the working assumption that makes prediction possible.

Voronoi and Thiessen polygons

  • ·Creates a surface of polygons (vector).
  • ·Assigns a value to the polygon that is equal to the value found at the nearest sample location.

Building them, step by step

Step 1: A set of sample points.

Step 2: Draw lines connecting the points to create a Delaunay triangulation.

Step 3: Find the bisectors of each line.

Step 4: Find where they intersect. Depending on the shape of the triangle, some may intersect within the triangle, outside of the triangle, or directly on an edge.

Step 5: Connect the dots following the bisectors. For the “rays,” follow the bisector that is perpendicular to the exterior triangle side.

Step 6: Erase construction lines.

Sampling density can affect accuracy, especially near the edge of the study area. The approach works well if points are relatively evenly distributed across the study area.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Conceptually the simplestAccuracy depends on sampling density
Ease of applicationBoundaries are abrupt, which can lead to abrupt changes
In class · point & call

Suppose we want to estimate the value at a brand-new, unmeasured location that falls inside one of the finished polygons above.

  1. What value does the Thiessen method assign to that location?
  2. What happens to the estimate the moment the location moves across the boundary into the next polygon?

1. It takes the value of that polygon’s own sample point — the single nearest measured point. Every location inside the polygon receives the same value.

2. The estimate jumps abruptly to the neighbor’s value the instant you cross the line. There is no gradual transition, which is exactly why Thiessen surfaces have hard, discontinuous boundaries.

Fixed radius

  • ·More complex than Voronoi/Thiessen.
  • ·Cell values are estimated based on the average of nearby samples.
  • ·The input is sampled points or observations (vector data) and the output is a raster surface.

Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW)

  • ·Estimates the values at unknown points using the distance and values to nearby points.
  • ·The weight of each sample point is an inverse proportion to the distance.
  • ·The further away the point, the less weight in helping define the unsampled location.

Calculation of the interpolated surface is based on two parameters:

  • 01The neighborhood that defines the area of points that are used to calculate unknown values, using a distance threshold or nearest neighbor.
  • 02The power exponent n of the distance, which defines the weight or influence that each known point will have when estimating unknown values.

Group brainstorm · work it out, then raise your hand

Three samples sit at the distances and values below. Estimate the value at the target with IDW at power n = 2, following the equation above: the numerator adds up each known value divided by its distancen (value ÷ dn), and the denominator adds up 1 ÷ dn. Work it out, then raise your hand — we’ll reveal the steps together.

SampleValue (z)Distance (d)
A101
B202
C305

1. Numerator — for each point, value ÷ dn (with n = 2), then add them up:
A = 10 ÷ 1² = 10.0  ·  B = 20 ÷ 2² = 5.0  ·  C = 30 ÷ 5² = 1.2
Sum = 10.0 + 5.0 + 1.2 = 16.2

2. Denominator — for each point, 1 ÷ dn, then add them up:
A = 1 ÷ 1² = 1.00  ·  B = 1 ÷ 2² = 0.25  ·  C = 1 ÷ 5² = 0.04
Sum = 1.00 + 0.25 + 0.04 = 1.29

3. Estimate = numerator ÷ denominator = 16.2 ÷ 1.29 ≈ 12.6

Notice the estimate sits close to A’s value of 10 — the nearest point dominated, exactly as inverse-distance weighting intends.

How the power exponent reshapes the surface

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Quick and computationally efficientConsiders distance between local points only in prediction (relies on spatial autocorrelation)
Works well with many data types
Models surface as continuous (no abrupt changes)

Model evaluation

Interpolation begins with points and ends with a surface.

It is ultimately an estimation. Methods, parameters, and input data will all have an impact on the accuracy of the output, and it’s important to measure this accuracy.

The performance of the interpolator can be summarized by computing the root-mean of squared residuals (RMSE) from the errors. A residual is simply the gap between a value the model predicts and the value actually measured there; RMSE rolls all of those gaps into a single number, in the same units as the data.

Other spatial interpolation methods

  • ·Kriging: A geostatistical method that not only considers the distance between known and unknown points but also accounts for the spatial autocorrelation in the data. Kriging involves modeling the spatial variance and then predicting values based on this model.
  • ·Splines: Fits a smooth surface through known points by minimizing the curvature. Splines are typically used to generate smooth surfaces and are especially useful for estimating gradual changes.

Key takeaways

1
Interpolation fills the gaps. Spatial interpolation helps estimate values at places where no sample was collected.
2
It leans on Tobler’s Law. Interpolation works best when nearby places are more similar than distant places.
3
Sampling is destiny. The quality of an interpolated surface depends heavily on the spacing and coverage of sample points.
4
Method shapes the surface. Different interpolation methods produce different kinds of surfaces, from abrupt boundaries to smoother continuous estimates.
5
Estimates need checking. Interpolated surfaces are estimates, so their accuracy should be checked rather than assumed.
